holding: As a result, Criminal Appeals No. 60892 of 2021 and Criminal Appeal No. 77604 of 2021 are accepted in toto. The conviction and sentence recorded by the trial court in its judgment dated 13.09.2021 are set aside, consequently ordering the acquittal of Imran Javed, son of Javed Iqbal, Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti and Haider Ali, son of Khan Tehseen Arshi, the appellants of the charges in case F.I.R. No. 1157 of 2016, dated 04.11.2016, registered under Sections 302, 365, 392, 34, 109, 411 PPC, at Police Station Shahdara Town, District Lahore. The appellants, Imran Javed, son of Javed Iqbal Khan, Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti and Haider Ali, son of Khan Tehseen Arshi, are in jail and are directed to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 12.10.2026. Appellants by: M/s Sikandar Zulqarnain Saleem and Mehram Ali Bali Advocates in Crl. Appeal No.60892 of 2021 and Mr. Anis Khan Sherwani, Advocate in Crl. Appeal No.77604 of 2021. State by: Mr. Muhammad Akhlaq, Additional Prosecutor General with Iftikhar D.S.P. and Naeem S.I. Complainant by: Complainant in person. -------------- AALIA NEELUM, CHIEF JUSTICE: (1) Imran Javed, son of Javed Iqbal, caste Awan, resident of Block-R, House No. 1, Johar Town, Lahore (appellant in Criminal Appeal No. 60892 of 2021); (2) Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti, caste Jatt, resident of Chak No. 219, Sahiwala, Tehsil and District Faisalabad; and (3) Haider Ali, son of Khan Tehseen Arshi, caste Jatt, resident of Chak No. 219, Sahiwala, Tehsil and District Faisalabad (appellants in Criminal Appeal No. 77604-J of 2021), were implicated in case F.I.R. No. 1157 of 2016, registered at Police Station Shahdara Town, District Lahore, for offences under sections 302, 365, 392, 34, 109 and 411 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860. They were tried by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Lahore, who, vide judgment dated 13.09.2021, convicted the appellants as follows: (Appellant in Crl. Appeal No.60892 of 2021) (i) Imran Javed: He was convicted under section 109 PPC read with section 302(b) PPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life as Tazir for abetting Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali in committing qatl-e-amd of deceased Shahbaz Ahmed. He was also directed to pay compensation of Rs.200,000/- (Rupees two hundred thousand) to each of the legal heirs of the deceased under section 544-A Cr.P.C. In default of payment of compensation, he was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for six months. He was further convicted under section 109 PPC read with section 392 PPC for abetting Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali in committing robbery against deceased Shahbaz Ahmed and sentenced to four years' simple imprisonment, along with a fine of Rs.50,000/-. In default of payment of fine, he was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for two months. He was also convicted under section 109 PPC read with section 365 PPC for abetting Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali in abducting deceased Shahbaz Ahmed and sentenced to four years' simple imprisonment, along with a fine of Rs.50,000/-. In default of payment of fine, he was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for two months. All the sentences were directed to run concurrently. He was also extended the benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C. (Appellants in Crl. Appeal No.77604-J of 2021) (ii) Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali: Both were convicted under section 302(b) PPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life as Tazir for committing the murder of deceased Shahbaz Ahmed. Each of them was also directed to pay compensation of Rs.200,000/- (Rupees two hundred thousand) to the legal heirs of the deceased under section 544-A Cr.P.C. In default of payment of compensation, each convict was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for six months. They were further convicted under section 392 PPC for committing robbery against deceased Shahbaz Ahmed and sentenced to four years' simple imprisonment each, along with a fine of Rs.50,000/- each. In default of payment of fine, each convict was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for two months. They were also convicted under section 365 PPC for abducting deceased Shahbaz Ahmed and sentenced to four years' simple imprisonment each, along with a fine of Rs.50,000/- each. In default of payment of fine, each convict was ordered to undergo simple imprisonment for two months. Furthermore, both were convicted under section 411 PPC and sentenced to two years' simple imprisonment each. All the sentences were directed to run concurrently. Both convicts were also extended the benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C.

Feeling aggrieved by the judgment of the learned trial court, Imran Javed has challenged his conviction by filing Criminal Appeal No. 60892 of 2021, whereas Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali have assailed their respective convictions through Criminal Appeal No. 77604-J of 2021. Since both appeals arise out of the same judgment, they are being decided through this single judgment.

The prosecution case, as set out in the F.I.R. (Ex.PM), lodged on the complaint (Ex.PE) of Mehmood Ali (PW-2), is that his brother, Shahbaz Ahmed, owned a taxi car, Toyota Corolla, bearing Registration No. LEC-10-7331, which he used to park at Shahdara Morr Taxi Stand. On 03.11.2016, at about 8:00 a.m., Shahbaz Ahmed took the said car to Shahdara Morr Taxi Stand but did not return. The complainant (PW-2) tried to contact him on his mobile phone No. 0300- 4858269; however, the same was found switched off. He then contacted the management of Shahdara Morr Taxi Stand, whose owner informed him that on the previous night, at about 9:00 p.m., Shahbaz Ahmed had taken two passengers, namely Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti, and his son, residents of House No. 5, Street No. 55, Sector G-9/1, Islamabad, bearing mobile phone No. 0322-8008453, who intended to transport their patient from Doctors Hospital to Millat Chowk, Faisalabad. The stand owner further informed the complainant that Shahbaz Ahmed had boarded the said passengers in his car and left with them but had not made contact since then. The complainant made repeated calls to the mobile phone numbers of his brother as well as Khan Tehseen Arshi, but both numbers were found switched off. Having developed a strong suspicion that his brother had been abducted by Khan Tehseen Arshi and others, the complainant got lodged the instant F.I.R., initially under section 365 PPC. It is noteworthy that, according to the record available on the file, Muhammad Rafique, son of Allah Ditta, caste Arain, resident of Street No. 2, Usman Town, Faisalabad, submitted an application (Ex.PO) at Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad, stating therein that on 04.11.2016, at about 6:30 a.m., while he was proceeding towards the graveyard and reached near Zakir Street, Ali Block, he noticed the dead body of an unidentified person lying in front of a house under construction. In the meantime, Muhammad Nawaz, son of Muhammad Siddique, and Muhammad Fareed, son of Muhammad Sarwar, also gathered at the spot. Muhammad Rafique further alleged that the said person had been murdered by unknown persons for unknown reasons. Based on the said application (Ex.PO), F.I.R. No. 1003 of 2016 (Ex.PO/1), dated 04.11.2016, was registered at Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad, and the investigation was entrusted to Muhammad Ameen, SI. Subsequently, on 06.11.2016, the complainant (PW-2) came to know through the taxi stand that the dead body of an unidentified person had been recovered at Faisalabad and was lying at Allied Hospital, Faisalabad. The complainant, accompanied by others, proceeded to Faisalabad and met Muhammad Ameen, SI, of Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad, who was in the process of having the post-mortem examination of the unidentified dead body conducted. After the post-mortem examination, the complainant and his companions identified the dead body as that of Shahbaz Ahmed, brother of the complainant. Consequently, offences under sections 302, 34 and 392 PPC were added to the case.

After registration of the case, the investigation of this case was conducted by Munir Ahmad S.I, PW-18. The appellants having found guilty, report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., was sent to the court of competent jurisdiction. On 29.11.2018, the trial court formally charge-sheeted the appellants, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In support of its version, the prosecution produced as many as nineteen (19) prosecution witnesses.

After the closure of prosecution evidence, the appellants were examined under Section 342 of Cr.P.C., wherein the appellants had neither opted to appear as their own witnesses in terms of Section 340 (2) Cr.P.C., nor to produce defence evidence. In response to a particular question of why this case was against them and why the PWs deposed against them, the appellants made the following deposition:- (Appellant-Imran Javed in Crl. Appeal No.60892 of 2021) “I am innocent. I have not concern with the occurrence. I belong to a very noble profession of Advocate. I have been falsely and wrongly implicated in this case. Even the complainant and other legal heirs of the deceased submitted an affidavit before the court of learned Add. Sessions Judge Lahore and also got recorded their statements before the learned court. As a result of these statements, I was released on post arrest bail by the learned court vide order dated 02.01.2017. I have no relation with the other co-accused persons and have been falsely roped in this case.” (Appellants in Crl. Appeal No.77604-J of 2021) Appellant Khan Tehseen Arshi: “I am totally innocent having no nexus with the alleged occurrence. I have been made scapegoat in this case. My CNIC copy has been used by some unknown persons. I have never rented a taxi from Taxi stand Shahdara Moor, Lahore. There is no direct or indirect evidence available against me which connects me with the alleged occurrence. The I.O of this case summoned me on 06.11.2016 to join the investigation and I appeared before the I.O but he detained me. On 07.11.2016, I was shown to the complainant and witnesses and later on were booked in this false case.” Appellant Haider Ali: “I am totally innocent having no nexus with the alleged occurrence. I have been made scapegoat in this case. My CNIC copy has been used by some unknown persons. I have never rented a taxi from Taxi stand Shahdara Moor, Lahore. There is no direct or indirect evidence available against me which connects me with the alleged occurrence. The I.O of this case summoned me on 06.11.2016 to join the investigation and I appeared before the I.O but he detained me. On 07.11.2016, I was shown to the complainant and witnesses and later on were booked in this false case.”

Upon recording the evidence and evaluating the same in the light of the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for both sides, the trial court found the prosecution to have established its case against the appellants beyond any shadow of reasonable doubt and, accordingly, convicted and sentenced them in the terms stated hereinabove.
I have heard the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the parties and have meticulously examined the record available on the file.

The prosecution case, as narrated by Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, is that his brother, Shahbaz Ahmed, used to drive a Toyota Corolla taxi bearing Registration No. LEC-10-7331 on a rental basis and went to Shahdara Morr Taxi Stand. On 03.11.2016, at about 8:00 a.m., Shahbaz Ahmed left for the taxi stand in his vehicle but did not return home at night. Consequently, Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant tried to contact him on his mobile phone No. 0300- 4858269, but the same was found switched off. The following morning i.e. 04.11.2016, Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, visited the Shahdara Morr Taxi Stand and inquired from its owner about his brother, Muhammad Shahbaz. The owner informed him that on the previous night, at about 9:00 p.m., a passenger, namely Khan Tehseen Arshi, accompanied by his son, had visited the taxi stand and hired the vehicle for transporting a patient from Doctors Hospital to Millat Chowk, Faisalabad. The mobile phone number of the said passenger was 0322-8008453. The complainant repeatedly called both his brother and the said passenger on their respective mobile numbers, but both phones remained switched off. Thereafter, at 7:35 p.m. on 04.11.2016, Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, submitted a written application (Ex.PE) to Abdul Majeed, ASI (PW-11), at Shell Petrol Pump, Shahdara More, Lahore, reporting his brother’s missing. Abdul Majeed A.S.I (PW-11) recorded the police proceedings (Ex.PE/1) and forwarded the application to the police station through Muhammad Waseem Constable/7742 (not cited as a PW) for registration of the F.I.R. Amanat Ali, ASI, registered the F.I.R. (Ex.PM) at 7:45 p.m. Since Amanat Ali had died, Abdul Majeed A.S.I (PW-11) verified his signatures by way of secondary evidence. The place of occurrence was approximately one kilometre from the police station. Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, failed to furnish any plausible explanation for the delay in reporting the missing of his brother to the police. In his examination-in-chief, he stated that “on the next day in the morning I went to taxi stand and inquired from owner taxi stand about my brother Muhammad Shahbaz. He told me that yesterday, at 09:00 p.m a passenger Khan Tahseen alongwith his son came at taxi stand and hired the taxi for taking the patient from doctor hospital to Millat Chowk Faisalabad. The phone number of that passenger was 0322-8008453. Thereafter I made call on this number as well as on number of my brother and both were found switched off. I gave an application Ex.PE to police for registration of FIR against Khan Tahseen and his son Haider Ali accused present in court.” Thus, the complainant had already acquired information regarding the persons who had hired the taxi and the circumstances in which his brother had left with them. However, he did not explain why, despite having acquired such information, he waited until 7:35 p.m. on 04.11.2016 to report the matter to the police. The delay in lodging the F.I.R., therefore, remains unexplained and calls for scrutiny while assessing the credibility of the prosecution case. Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, stated during his examination-in-chief that on 04.11.2016, while serving as In-charge, Investigation Cell, Police Station Shahdara Town, he, along with other police officials, proceeded to the place of occurrence in connection with the investigation of this case. In the presence of Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, and four other persons he inspected the taxi stand situated at Shahdara Morr, Lahore, prepared a site plan of the place of occurrence and recorded the statements of the witnesses. On the same day, he did not record the statement of Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17), the owner of the taxi stand. Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer further deposed during examination-in-chief that on 05.11.2016, he again visited the taxi stand, where he met with Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17), who produced the relevant register of the taxi stand. After checking the register, Muhammad Rafiq handed over a photocopy thereof (Ex. P8) to him (the Investigating Officer), who took the same into possession through recovery memo (Ex.PK). Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17), in his examination-in-chief, stated that he was operating the taxi stand where drivers used to park their vehicles. He explained the procedure for booking a taxi, stating that whenever a vehicle was hired by a passenger, the particulars of the person hiring the vehicle, including his name, CNIC number, address and mobile phone number, were entered in the relevant register. He (PW-17) stated that on 03.11.2016, at about 8:45 p.m., Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali hired Shahbaz Ahmed’s taxi from his stand, and he recorded their particulars in the register. He had no further contact with Shahbaz Ahmed thereafter. The following day, all drivers at the stand informed him that Shahbaz Ahmed’s whereabouts were unknown, as he had not returned since the previous night and his mobile phone was switched off. The deceased’s parents/relatives subsequently made similar inquiries. In these circumstances, he learned that Shahbaz Ahmed had allegedly been abducted. Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer recorded his statement on 05.11.2016. Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17) deposed during cross- examination that: “I and my Munshi Malik Ijaz worked at the taxi stand. I remained at taxi stand for 12 hours and for the remaining twelve hours my Munshi remained at the taxi stand. My duty started from 08:00 a.m, to 08:00 p.m.” In his examination-in-chief, Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17) stated that Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali visited the taxi stand and hired the vehicle on 03.11.2016 at about 8:45 p.m. In cross-examination, however, he stated that his duty hours were from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. He neither explained who was present at the stand at 8:45 p.m. nor how he identified the person with whom the booking was made. This omission is material to assess the reliability of his testimony concerning the appellants’ alleged hiring of the taxi. Further, Muhammad Rafiq (PW-17) did not state in his examination-in- chief that Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant, met him on 04.11.2016 or that he provided Mehmood Ali (PW-2), the complainant with information about his brother.

The photocopy of the taxi stands register (Ex. P8) had no independent evidentiary value. However, the learned trial court failed to appreciate that the document produced before it was merely a photocopy of the alleged register and that the original register had not been produced during the trial. Merely assigning an exhibit number to a photocopy does not, by itself, establish its admissibility or prove the contents thereof in accordance with law.

The party relying upon such document is still required to prove its execution and contents in accordance with the provisions of the Qanoon- e-Shahdat Order, 1984 through admissible evidence. Thus, unless duly proved in accordance with the Qanoon-e-Shahdat Order, 1984 the contents of such documents cannot be relied upon by the Court. In the present case, Ex. P8 is a bare photocopy. It is not marked as Original, Seen and Returned, a requirement confirming that a valid original document was produced before the Court, compared with the copy on record, and returned to the holder, with the copy being retained as part of the record. The Original, Seen and Returned endorsement is a certification of the authenticity of the copy as a faithful reproduction of the original. Its absence, coupled with the complete non-production of the original, means that Ex. P8 cannot be relied upon as proof of the entry related to booking of the vehicle on 03.11.2016 by the accused persons i.e. Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali. Furthermore, the said document (Ex. P8) does not establish that, on 03.11.2016, the vehicle of Shahbaz Ahmed, the deceased, had been hired by the appellants. Thus, the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex. P8), in the absence of the original record and reliable proof of its contents, does not furnish independent corroboration of the prosecution's allegation regarding the alleged hiring of the vehicle by the appellants i.e. Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali.

Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, deposed during his examination-in-chief that, after taking into possession the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex. P8), he visited the CRO Branch and obtained the record of Khan Tehseen alias Arshi on the basis of his CNIC number, according to which his particulars were found to be correct. However, the document allegedly obtained from the CRO Branch was neither produced nor proved before the trial court. Furthermore, no prosecution witness was examined to establish as to who had supplied the said information to Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), or when it was furnished. Therefore, the CNIC number mentioned in the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex. P8) could not, by itself, establish that it belonged to Khan Tehseen alias Arshi. Similarly, during the investigation, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), obtained the call data and tracking record of mobile phone numbers 0323-4720662 and 0316-8073031, allegedly belonging to Haider Ali and Imran Javed, respectively. In this regard, Ghulam Murtaza 20555/C (PW-6), in his examination-in-chief, deposed about the collection of data on 08.12.2016. However, the prosecution failed to establish that the aforesaid mobile phone numbers actually belonged to Haider Ali and Imran Javed, respectively, as no representative of the concerned cellular mobile company was produced as a witness, nor was any certificate from the relevant service provider brought on record to establish that the said numbers had been issued in their names. Likewise, the prosecution also failed to establish that the mobile phone number 0322-8008453 mentioned in the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex.P8) belonged to Khan Tehseen Arshi. No evidence was collected by Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), to establish the ownership of the said number. Consequently, the prosecution failed to establish any reliable evidentiary link connecting the appellants, Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali, with the alleged hiring of the taxi or the incriminating material collected during the investigation. In these circumstances, the prosecution failed to establish that the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex. P8) pertained to the alleged booking transaction dated 03.11.2016 or that the particulars recorded therein, purportedly relating to Khan Tehseen Arshi, were correct. Consequently, the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex. P8), even if taken into consideration, failed to establish any reliable connection between its contents and the appellants, Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali.

Astonishingly, it is noted that Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, did not depose in his deposition that, on the basis of the particulars of the accused persons recorded in the photocopy of the taxi stand register (Ex.P8), he had made any effort to arrest Khan Tehseen Arshi to obtain information regarding the whereabouts of Shahbaz Ahmed, who was then missing, or to recover him. On the contrary, Mehmood Ali, SI (PW-2), the complainant, deposed in his examination-in-chief that on 06.11.2016, he came to know through the taxi stand that the dead body of an unidentified person had been recovered at Faisalabad and was lying at Allied Hospital, Faisalabad. Upon receiving this information, he, accompanied by Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) and Muhammad Riaz (give-up PW), proceeded to Faisalabad, where they approached the local police. Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) also furnished a similar account in his examination-in-chief.

However, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, narrated a somewhat different sequence of events. According to him, on 06.11.2016, the complainant joined the investigation along with his “maternal niece” and informed him that a dead body had been recovered within the jurisdiction of Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad. On receiving this information, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), accompanied by the complainant (PW-2) and other persons, proceeded to Faisalabad. Upon reaching the police station Sargodha Road Faisalabad, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18) deposed that he received following information: “The Moharrar of P.S Sargodha road Faisal abad told that a case FIR No.1003/16 dated 04.11.2016 u/s 302 PPC P.S Sargodha road Faisalabad was registered against unknown person and investigation was being carried by Muhammad Ameen SI who had proceeded to Allied hospital Faisalabad for the post mortem examination, the complainant Mehmood Ahmed, Muhammad Riaz and Faisal Ibrahim identified the dead body of deceased as Shahbaz, real brother of the complainant.” Whereas Muhammad Ameen Inspector (PW-13) deposed contrary to the deposition of Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18) as under: - “On 06.11.2016, Asif Jahan joined the investigation before me and produced before me scaled site plan in triplicate on which notes with red ink are of my handwriting. On the same day, I alongwith Fazal-e- Haq constable reached at Allied hospital Faisal abad where the dead body of deceased and other police papers were already deposited. At the same time, Munir Ahmed SI Incharge Investigation P.S Shahdra town Lahore alongwith Mehmood Ali. Muhammad Riaz and Faisal Ibrahim PWs joined the investigation before me in the hospital, the doctor showed the dead body of the deceased to Mehmood Ali, Faisal Ibrahim which was identified by them who identified the dead body as Shahbaz (brother of Mehmood Ali and Mamo of Riaz and Faisal Ibrahim (PWs).”

A perusal of F.I.R. No. 1003 of 2016 (Ex.PO/1) reveals that the dead body of an unidentified person had been recovered on 04.11.2016, at about 6:30 a.m. Astonishingly, despite the fact that the deceased was unidentified and, as recorded in the F.I.R., had sustained a firearm injury to his head, his post-mortem examination was not conducted immediately. Instead, the dead body was kept in the mortuary refrigerator, and its post- mortem examination was conducted by Dr. Javed Iqbal (PW-16) on 06.11.2016 at 12:15 p.m. According to Muhammad Ameen Inspector (PW- 13), the post-mortem examination was conducted after identification of the dead body. This circumstance assumes significance when examined in the light of the statement of Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, particularly his testimony in which the complainant and other witnesses identified the dead body in relation to the arrival of Muhammad Ameen, SI, at Allied Hospital, Faisalabad, and the time of conducting of the post-mortem examination.

A perusal of the post-mortem report (Ex. PV) further reveals that the name and parentage of the deceased were recorded as unknown in the relevant columns. It is, indeed, a strange coincidence that Muhammad Ameen, Inspector (PW-15), visited Allied Hospital, Faisalabad, on 06.11.2016 for the post-mortem examination of the dead body, while, on the very same day, Mehmood Ali (PW-2) came to know about the presence of an unidentified dead body at Allied Hospital, Faisalabad. Thereafter, he, along with Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) and other witnesses, informed Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, who also reached Allied Hospital, Faisalabad, on the same day. The aforesaid circumstances, when considered collectively, give rise to serious questions regarding the prosecution's version of events. Of particular significance is the fact that Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, did not undertake any independent investigation to ascertain the circumstances surrounding the recovery, identification and post-mortem examination of the dead body. These material aspects further cast doubt on the prosecution's account, particularly regarding the timing and circumstances in which the post- mortem examination was conducted. It is noteworthy that Muhammad Ameen, Inspector (PW-13), the Investigating Officer of case F.I.R. No. 1003 of 2016 (Ex.PO/1), did not have the post-mortem examination of the dead body conducted until 06.11.2016, despite its recovery on 04.11.2016. This delay resulted in the loss of an important piece of evidence. Dr. Javed Iqbal (PW-16), in his examination-in-chief, stated that the interval between the infliction of the injury and death was immediate; however, he could not specify the interval between death and the post-mortem examination, as the dead body had been kept in a refrigerator. Thus, owing to the delayed post- mortem examination, an important piece of medical evidence, namely the time elapsed between death and the post-mortem examination, could not be ascertained. This omission deprived the Court of potentially significant evidence relevant to the determination of the chronology of events.

The prosecution also relied upon the last seen evidence, seeking to establish that Shahbaz Ahmed, the deceased, was seen in the company of the appellants shortly before his abduction. Maqsood Ahmed (PW-7) deposed that on 03.11.2016, between approximately 8:00/9:00 p.m., he was present at the taxi stand near Shell Petrol Pump, Shahdara Morr, Lahore, along with Matloob Khan (not cited as PW), Muhammad Saleem (not cited as PW), Naveed Ahmed (not cited as PW) and Muhammad Shahbaz (not cited as PW). According to him, two persons, whom he subsequently knew as Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali, appellants, hired the taxi driven by the deceased for a journey to Doctors Hospital, Lahore, and thereafter to Faisalabad. They obtained a ticket and had their names entered in the relevant register before leaving. Maqsood Ahmed (PW-7) claimed that he was present at Shahdara Morr, near Shell Petrol Pump, Lahore, where the accused persons allegedly got their names entered in the register and obtained a ticket. Contrary to the deposition of Maqsood Ahmad (PW-7), Matloob Ahmad Khan (PW-16), in his examination-in-chief, deposed, in his presence, the accused persons, namely Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali, came to Shahdara Chowk, near the petrol pump, and sought to hire a car for transporting a patient from Doctors Hospital, Lahore, to Faisalabad. According to him, the fare was settled with Shahbaz Ahmad, the deceased, at Rs.4,500/-. Thereafter, Shahbaz Ahmad proceeded towards Doctors Hospital along with the accused persons after paying Rs.50/- to the caretaker of the taxi stand in his presence. This assertion introduced a new and material fact into the prosecution case. However, the person who allegedly issued the ticket, received the payment, and made the entries in the register was not produced as a witness to substantiate this part of the prosecution version. Furthermore, Maqsood Ahmed (PW-7) admitted during cross- examination that he did not know the accused persons prior to the occurrence and had met them at the police station. He (PW-7) failed to explain how, when, or through whom he came to know their names. This omission assumes significance, particularly when the prosecution relies upon his testimony to establish the identity of the persons who allegedly hired the taxi. In the absence of the testimony of the person who issued the ticket and recorded the particulars in the register, the assertion of Maqsood Ahmed (PW-7) regarding the alleged booking transaction remains without independent corroboration. Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8), sister’s husband of Shahbaz Ahmad deceased, in his examination-in-chief, deposed that on 03.11.2016, he was waiting for passengers near Shell Petrol Pump, Shahdara Morr. Abdul Majeed (PW-9) also reached there between approximately 8:00/9:00 p.m., after completing his work at the Wood Market, Lahore. According to Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8), the deceased was present with his taxi and two persons: one aged about 60 years, whom he identified as Khan Tehseen Arshi, and the other aged about 20 to 22 years, whom he identified as Haider Ali. Upon inquiry, the deceased told him that he was proceeding to Faisalabad. He further deposed that Imran Javed, appellant, also boarded the vehicle, whereafter they departed together. Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8), deposed during cross-examination that: “The distance between me and the car of deceased was about thirty feet.” Furthermore, the version narrated by Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8) does not appear to be a natural conduct. It is not possible to engage in a conversation with someone regarding his destination from approximately thirty feet. Such an alleged exchange, in the circumstances narrated by the witness, does not appeal to the ordinary course of human conduct and, therefore, renders his testimony less convincing. The testimony of Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8) likewise calls for scrutiny. Although he claimed to have witnessed on 03.11.2016 leaving Shahbaz Ahmad deceased with the appellants, but fact remains that he joined the investigation only on 07.11.2016 and did not furnish the names or particulars of the persons allegedly accompanying the deceased to the Investigating Officer during the intervening period. He also failed to explain before the Court how he had come to know their names. These omissions bear upon the credibility of his testimony and the reliability of his identification of the appellants. This circumstance, particularly in the absence of any plausible explanation for such conduct, makes the prosecution's version regarding the alleged last-seen evidence difficult to accept without independent and reliable corroboration. On a cumulative appraisal, the unexplained basis of identification in the testimony of both witnesses, coupled with Muhammad Ilyas’s belated disclosure to the Investigating Officer, renders the alleged last-seen circumstance doubtful and lost its evidentiary value, therefore, it does not provides a reliable link connecting the appellants with the deceased’s abduction. In the absence of independent corroboration of the booking transaction, these discrepancies also have a bearing on the weight to be attached to their respective accounts of the deceased having left in the company of the accused persons.

As regards the recovery of the car bearing Registration No. LEC- 7331-10 (P-4) and the blood-stained Danda (P-5), allegedly effected at the instance of Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali from the house of Imran Javed, situated at Jinnah Colony, Jauharabad, District Khushab, the prosecution case, as emerging from the statements of Mehmood Ali (PW-2), Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) and Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, is that, upon receiving information that an unidentified dead body had been recovered within the jurisdiction of Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad, they proceeded to Allied Hospital, Faisalabad, on 06.11.2016, where the complainant and other witnesses identified the dead body as that of Shahbaz Ahmad. This circumstance, when read alongside the contents of F.I.R. No. 1003 of 2016 (Ex.PO/1), registered on 04.11.2016 under section 302 PPC at Police Station Sargodha Road, Faisalabad, indicates that the deceased was murdered at Faisalabad. The said F.I.R. was initially registered against unknown accused persons at Faisalabad. In this context, the prosecution was required to establish a reliable connection between the deceased, the recovered vehicle and the place from where the alleged recovery was affected. However, the registration book of the vehicle was not produced to establish that car bearing Registration No. LEC-7331-10 (P-4) was owned by Shahbaz Ahmad, the deceased. Furthermore, Muhammad Ilyas (PW-8), who is the husband of the deceased's sister, stated during cross-examination that, “The car was perhaps Honda manufactured.” This statement also assumes relevance in assessing the identification and ownership of the recovered vehicle. Although the prosecution evidence suggests that Shahbaz Ahmad was engaged in the business of running a rent-a-car service, it does not, without further evidence, establish that he was the owner of the vehicle allegedly recovered. Thus, the ownership of the recovered vehicle and its connection with the deceased remained matters requiring proof. Furthermore, the place of the alleged recovery also requires examination. In this regard, Mehmood Ali (PW-2), during cross-examination, stated that: “The key of the house was with a person at general store infront of that house. The I.O had recorded the statement of the person working at the said general store.” Contrary to the deposition of Mehmood Ali (PW-2), Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) deposed during his examination-in-chief that: “We reached above said place at 3:00 pm, the accused persons deboarded from the vehicle collected key of house from a nearby General store and opened the door of house and got recovered Car No. LEC 7331 of the deceased.”

The statements of the prosecution witnesses also reveal a discrepancy regarding the way the house was opened at the time of the alleged recovery. Mehmood Ali (PW-2), stated that they themselves opened the door, whereas Faisal Ibrahim (PW-4) deposed that, upon their arrival at the spot, the accused persons obtained the keys of the house from a general store, opened its door and got the vehicle recovered. On the other hand, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, did not specify in his examination-in-chief who opened the door of the house. Thus, the prosecution witnesses have not given a consistent testimony of a material circumstance relating to the alleged recovery. This discrepancy assumes significance because the prosecution relies upon the alleged recovery of the vehicle (P-4) and the blood-stained Danda (P-5) from the said premises at the instance of the accused persons. The absence of a clear and consistent account of how the premises were accessed calls for cautious scrutiny of the recovery proceedings and the evidentiary value to be attached to them. These omissions assume significance in assessing the manner and circumstances of the alleged recoveries. In addition, the person at general store, from whom the key of the house was collected was the star witness. However, the prosecution has not produced him as a witness. Therefore, an adverse inference is to be drawn within the meaning of Article 129 (g) of Qanun-e-Shahadat, Order 1984, that had the person at general store was produced, he would have been unfavorable to the prosecution. Reliance is placed on the case reported as “The State and others v. Abdul Khaliq and others” (PLD 2011 SC 554). In these circumstances, the recoveries of vehicle (P-4) and the blood-stained Danda (P-5) from a house whose ownership or connection with Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali was never established has no evidentiary value.

As far as recoveries of Danda blood-stained (P-5) on the pointing of Khan Tahseen, on 04.12.2016 and positive report of Punjab Forensic Science Agency (Ex.PDD) is concerned, as per the prosecution case, Munir Ahmad S.I (PW-18)-the investigating officer, on 04.12.2016, recovered the Danda blood- stained (P-5) on the pointing of Khan Tahseen (the appellant), which was taken into possession through the sealed parcel and same was deposited with the office of Punjab Forensic Science Agency. Per the Punjab Forensic Science Agency report (Ex.PDD), human blood was identified on item # 1.1, i.e., “Danda recovered from Khan Tahseen.” It has been noticed that the recovered Danda was analyzed on 04.01.2017, about 02-months after the occurrence. Human blood was not compared with Shahbaz Ahmad's blood. It was not possible to determine the origin of the blood on “Danda”, as blood disintegrated after one month of the occurrence and in this regard, case of “FAISAL MEHMOOD. Vs. THE STATE” (2017 Cr.LJ 1) can be referred and relevant portion from the same is reproduced hereunder:- “It was scientifically impossible to detect the origin of the blood after about two years of the occurrence because human blood disintegrates in a period of about three weeks.” The alleged recovery of the vehicle (P-4) and the blood-stained danda (P-5) also does not appear to be consistent with the ordinary course of human conduct. As reflected in F.I.R. No. 1003 of 2016 (Ex.PO/1), the dead body of an unidentified person was recovered at Faisalabad, where the said F.I.R. was also registered. The prosecution evidence, therefore, indicates that the murder took place at Faisalabad. In these circumstances, it is difficult to comprehend why the accused persons, after allegedly committing the murder at Faisalabad, would preserve the blood- stained Danda and transport it all the way to Jauharabad, District Khushab, to keep it concealed in a house, thereby retaining an incriminating piece of evidence that could subsequently be used against them. Where the perpetrators had allegedly taken such precautions as to conceal the identity of the accused and avoid detection of the crime, their alleged act of preserving and keeping the very weapon used in the offence appears unusual and requires convincing corroboration. Furthermore, as already discussed, the prosecution did not examine the person present at the general store situated opposite the house, from whom the keys of the premises were allegedly obtained. His testimony could have assisted the Court in determining who was in possession of the house, who occupied the house, whether Khan Tehseen Arshi and Haider Ali resided there, and whether the premises belonged to Imran Javed. No reliable documentary or oral evidence was otherwise produced to establish the ownership or possession of the house from which the alleged recoveries were affected. Similarly, Munir Ahmed, SI (PW-18), the Investigating Officer, did not produce or prove any independent evidence during the trial to establish either the ownership of the recovered vehicle or the ownership or possession of the premises in question.

In these circumstances, the prosecution has not satisfactorily established the connection of the recovered vehicle (P-4) and the blood-stained Danda (P-5) with the accused persons or the crime in question. The deficiencies in proof of the ownership and possession of the premises, coupled with the unexplained circumstances surrounding the alleged concealment and recovery of the articles, materially affect the evidentiary value of the recovery proceedings and give rise to doubt regarding the prosecution's version. Even otherwise, it does not appeal to reason that the accused might have kept blood-stained Danda (P-5) with him intact to produce the same before the Investigating Officer on his arrest. In these circumstances, the recoveries and positive report are not of any consequence.

From the facts and circumstances narrated above, I am convinced that the prosecution could not prove its case against the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, as there are numerous inconsistencies in the prosecution's story. The accused persons are not required to prove their innocence completely. If the prosecution's story is uncertain, then the benefit of the doubt must be given to the accused-appellant. In light of this, it can be concluded that the prosecution has significantly failed to establish the guilt of the accused/appellants, and the conviction reached by the trial court under these circumstances contradicts established principles of law recognized for the administration of criminal justice. According to the law, the benefit of every doubt will be granted in favor of the accused/appellant. The conviction and sentence imposed by the trial court cannot be upheld. Reference has been made to the case reported as Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230), where the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan held that even a single circumstance creating reasonable doubts in a prudent mind about the guilt of the accused entitles him to its benefit, not as a matter of grace and concession, but as a matter of right.

As a result, Criminal Appeals No. 60892 of 2021 and Criminal Appeal No. 77604 of 2021 are accepted in toto. The conviction and sentence recorded by the trial court in its judgment dated 13.09.2021 are set aside, consequently ordering the acquittal of Imran Javed, son of Javed Iqbal, Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti and Haider Ali, son of Khan Tehseen Arshi, the appellants of the charges in case F.I.R. No. 1157 of 2016, dated 04.11.2016, registered under Sections 302, 365, 392, 34, 109, 411 PPC, at Police Station Shahdara Town, District Lahore. The appellants, Imran Javed, son of Javed Iqbal Khan, Khan Tehseen Arshi, son of Nazir Hussain Chishti and Haider Ali, son of Khan Tehseen Arshi, are in jail and are directed to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.
